edges.rationale: Analyzing how HTTP uses TCP connections (one object per connection vs. multiple objects) and computing response times requires first understanding that HTTP is a stateless request-response protocol for fetching objects referenced by a web page.
Request lines, methods, status lines, and status codes only make sense once the student knows the HTTP client/server request-response model and what browsers ask of web servers.
Cookies are explicitly presented as a mechanism for adding stateful user identification on top of HTTP's stateless model, so the stateless request-response model must be learned first.
Understanding proxy servers, cache hits/misses, and serving HTTP requests on behalf of clients presupposes knowledge of the browser/server request-response model and web objects.
HTTP/2's improvements (multiplexing, head-of-line blocking, page-load latency) are meaningful only against the baseline HTTP/1.x request-response model and the multi-object structure of web pages.
Two of the four cookie components are HTTP header lines (cookie-setting and cookie-carrying headers), so understanding message headers is needed to grasp how cookies work.
The conditional GET for keeping cached copies fresh is a specific use of HTTP request messages with header lines (If-Modified-Since), which requires knowing the request message structure first.
HTTP/2's multiplexing of many requests/responses over a single TCP connection and its handling of head-of-line blocking build directly on the persistent-connection model and its latency limitations.

HTTP/2's framing mechanism decomposes and restructures classic HTTP request/response messages into frames, so the traditional message format must be understood first to appreciate what framing changes.
